points.title: Threats to data
points.must: The main threats: hackers / unauthorised access, malware, physical events (fire, flood, power cut, hardware failure) and careless users; several layers of protection are needed.

points.title: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
points.must: Confidentiality (only authorised people read the data), integrity (data correct, changed only by authorised people) and availability (system usable when needed).

points.title: Physical risks and countermeasures
points.must: At least four physical risks, each with a countermeasure: theft (locks, CCTV), fire (gas fire suppression), flood (servers off the floor), power cut (UPS), overheating (air conditioning), hardware failure (RAID).

points.title: UPS
points.must: A UPS has a battery that keeps computers running in a power cut so work is saved and the system shuts down safely; a surge protector only stops voltage spikes.

points.title: What a firewall is
points.must: Hardware or software between the network and the Internet that checks every data packet against security rules and allows or blocks it.

points.title: What a firewall checks
points.must: Source / destination IP address, port number and protocol; it can block websites or applications and logs connection attempts.

points.title: Limits of a firewall
points.must: It cannot stop malware that comes through allowed channels (e-mail attachments, USB sticks) or insiders, and it must be configured correctly.

points.title: Firewall types and rules
points.must: Hardware (whole network) vs software (one computer) firewall; rules are checked from the top, the first match decides, and everything else is blocked.

points.title: Encryption
points.must: Plaintext is turned into ciphertext with an algorithm and a key; only someone with the key can decrypt it; it does not stop theft but makes stolen data unreadable.

points.title: Symmetric encryption
points.must: The same secret key encrypts and decrypts; it is fast (used for disks, files, Wi-Fi); the key must be shared secretly (key distribution problem); e.g. AES (DES is old and broken).

points.title: Asymmetric encryption
points.must: A key pair: the receiver's public key encrypts, only the matching private key decrypts; slower; solves the key-sharing problem; e.g. RSA; used in HTTPS key exchange and digital signatures.

points.title: Uses of encryption
points.must: HTTPS (uses both kinds), full-disk encryption, Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3), end-to-end messaging; lost key = lost data.

points.title: Caesar cipher
points.must: Each letter is shifted by the key; only 25 keys, so it is broken by brute force.

points.title: Types of threats
points.must: Several named threats with what happens, e.g. phishing, pharming, denial of service, interception, social engineering; internal vs external or accidental vs deliberate.

points.title: How a firewall decides
points.must: Packet filtering (IP address, port), stateful inspection (only replies to connections from inside) and/or proxy firewall (fetches pages, checks content).

points.title: Key length; at rest and in transit
points.must: Longer keys mean many more possible keys, so brute force takes far longer (DES 56-bit broken, AES 128/256-bit safe); data at rest (disk encryption) vs in transit (HTTPS, Wi-Fi, VPN).

points.title: Digital signatures, certificates, hashing
points.must: A signature is made with the sender's private key and checked with their public key (proves sender and integrity); a certificate links a public key to a website; a hash is one-way with no key (passwords stored as hashes).
